claim: RNA binding proteins (RBPs) containing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) are present in diverse molecular complexes where they function as dynamic regulators.
source: RNA binding proteins (RBPs) containing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) are present in diverse molecular complexes where they function as dynamic regulators.
evidence: This is a general statement about RBPs with IDRs based on established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: IDR-RBPs promote liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and the formation of membraneless organelles such as stress granules and nucleoli.
source: Their characteristics promote liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and the formation of membraneless organelles such as stress granules and nucleoli.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific understanding of IDR-RBP properties.

claim: IDR-RBPs are particularly relevant in the nervous system and their dysfunction is associated with neurodegenerative diseases and brain tumor development.
source: IDR-RBPs are particularly relevant in the nervous system and their dysfunction is associated with neurodegenerative diseases and brain tumor development.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: SERBP1 is mostly disordered and lacks canonical RNA-binding domains.
source: Serpine1 mRNA-binding protein 1 (SERBP1) is a unique member of this group, being mostly disordered and lacking canonical RNA-binding domains.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work (Baudin et al., 2021) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: SERBP1 participates in pathological stress granules and Tau aggregates in Alzheimer's brains.
source: We defined SERBP1's interactome, uncovered novel roles in splicing, cell division and ribosomal biogenesis, and showed its participation in pathological stress granules and Tau aggregates in Alzheimer's brains.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including immunofluorescence and PLA assays shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: SERBP1 preferentially interacts with other G-quadruplex (G4) binders implicated in different stages of gene expression.
source: SERBP1 preferentially interacts with other G-quadruplex (G4) binders, implicated in different stages of gene expression, suggesting that G4 binding is a critical component of SERBP1 function in different settings.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data showing that 38% of SERBP1-associated proteins are G4 binders, as shown in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 6.

claim: SERBP1 interacts with PARP1 and its associated factors and influences PARylation.
source: SERBP1 interacts with PARP1 and its associated factors and influences PARylation.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches including IP-Western, in vitro PARylation assays, and pulldown experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Protein complexes in which SERBP1 participates contain mostly PARylated proteins and PAR binders.
source: Moreover, protein complexes in which SERBP1 participates contain mostly PARylated proteins and PAR binders.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data showing that circa 56% of SERBP1 interactors get PARylated and/or bind PAR, as shown in Figure 4F.

claim: SERBP1 influences PARP1 function and PARylation, while PARylation modulates SERBP1 functions and participation in regulatory complexes.
source: Based on these results, we propose a feedback regulatory model in which SERBP1 influences PARP1 function and PARylation, while PARylation modulates SERBP1 functions and participation in regulatory complexes.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on inference from multiple experimental observations including PARylation assays, pulldown experiments, and PARP inhibitor studies.

claim: There are 1500 RBP members cataloged in the human genome.
source: RNA binding proteins (RBPs) are a diverse group of regulators with 1500 members cataloged in the human genome (Gerstberger et al., 2014; Corley et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RBPs control multiple stages of gene expression, including RNA processing, modification, transport, decay, localization, and translation.
source: They display a variety of RNA binding domains (RRMs, zinc-fingers, KH domains, dsRBD, etc.) and control multiple stages of gene expression, including RNA processing (splicing, capping, 3' end processing, and polyadenylation), modification, transport, decay, localization, and translation (Corley et al., 2020; Kelaini et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RBPs are particularly relevant in the nervous system, where they regulate critical aspects of neurogenesis, neuronal function, and nervous system development.
source: RBPs are particularly relevant in the nervous system, where they regulate critical aspects of neurogenesis, neuronal function, and nervous system development (Chan et al., 2022; Bryant and Yazdani, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Alterations in RBP expression and function are linked to neurological disorders, neurodegenerative diseases, and brain tumor development.
source: Alterations in RBP expression and function are linked to neurological disorders, neurodegenerative diseases, and brain tumor development (Prashad and Gopal, 2021; Marcelino Meliso et al., 2017; Sanya et al., 2023; Kavanagh et al., 2022; Velasco et al., 2019; Gebauer et al., 2021; Nussbacher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: RBP interactions can take place in the context of macromolecular complexes associated with liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS).
source: RBP interactions can take place in the context of macromolecular complexes associated with liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS).
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: LLPS supports important regulatory environments and is the foundation for membraneless organelles such as stress granules, Cajal bodies, nucleoli, and P-bodies.
source: This process supports important regulatory environments and is the foundation for membraneless organelles such as stress granules, Cajal bodies, nucleoli, and P-bodies (An et al., 2021; Drino and Schaefer, 2018; Gomes and Shorter, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RBPs in LLPS tend to share characteristics that include intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and RGG boxes.
source: RBPs in LLPS tend to share characteristics that include intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and RGG boxes.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: IDR-RBPs can interact with RNA without the presence of specific folded RNA-binding domains.
source: IDR-RBPs can interact with RNA without the presence of specific folded RNA-binding domains (Zeke et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: IDR-RBPs provide unique structural and biophysical characteristics to dynamically regulate translation, stress response, RNA processing, and neuronal function.
source: These features provide unique structural and biophysical characteristics to dynamically regulate translation, stress response, RNA processing, and neuronal function (Roden and Gladfelter, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Many RBPs in LLPS share a binding preference for G-quadruplexes (G4s).
source: Many RBPs in LLPS share a binding preference for G-quadruplexes (G4s).
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: G4s are complex DNA or RNA structures that display stacked tetrads of guanosines stabilized by Hoogsteen base pairing.
source: G4s are complex DNA or RNA structures that display stacked tetrads of guanosines stabilized by Hoogsteen base pairing.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about G4 structure.

claim: G4s function as regulatory elements in different stages of gene expression, promote LLPS, and are implicated in cancer, viral replication, neurodegenerative diseases, neurological disorders, and prion diseases.
source: They function as regulatory elements in different stages of gene expression, promote LLPS, and are implicated in cancer, viral replication, neurodegenerative diseases, neurological disorders, and prion diseases (Cave and Willis, 2022; Masai and Tanaka, 2020; Nakanishi and Seimiya, 2020; Kosiol et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RBPs containing IDRs and RGG motifs are particularly relevant in the nervous system.
source: RBPs containing IDRs and RGG motifs are particularly relevant in the nervous system.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Misfolding of RBPs containing IDRs and RGG motifs contributes to the formation of pathological protein aggregates in Alzheimer's disease (AD), Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration (FTLD), Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), and Parkinson's disease (PD).
source: Their misfolding contributes to the formation of pathological protein aggregates in Alzheimer's disease (AD), Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration (FTLD), Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), and Parkinson's disease (PD) while their aberrant expression has been linked to glioblastoma development (Darling and Shorter, 2021; Webber et al., 2020; Uversky, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Aberrant expression of RBPs containing IDRs and RGG motifs has been linked to glioblastoma development.
source: Their misfolding contributes to the formation of pathological protein aggregates in Alzheimer's disease (AD), Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration (FTLD), Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), and Parkinson's disease (PD) while their aberrant expression has been linked to glioblastoma development (Darling and Shorter, 2021; Webber et al., 2020; Uversky, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SERBP1 is a unique member of IDR-RBPs for being mostly disordered and lacking typical RNA binding domains other than two short RG/RGG motifs.
source: SERBP1 (Serpine1 mRNA-binding protein 1) is a unique member of this group of RBPs for being mostly disordered and lacking typical RNA binding domains other than two short RG/RGG motifs (Baudin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: SERBP1 is a highly conserved protein with homologs identified in yeast, plants, invertebrates, and vertebrates.
source: SERBP1 is a highly conserved protein with homologs identified in yeast, plants, invertebrates, and vertebrates.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about SERBP1 conservation.

claim: SERBP1 is highly expressed in neuronal and glioma stem cells and a decrease in its levels is required for neuronal differentiation.
source: SERBP1 is highly expressed in neuronal and glioma stem cells and a decrease in its levels is required for neuronal differentiation (Kosti et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In glioblastoma, SERBP1 functions as a central regulator of metabolic pathways, coordinating the expression of related enzymes and associated factors implicated in serine biosynthesis, one-carbon, and 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA) cycles.
source: In glioblastoma, SERBP1 functions as a central regulator of metabolic pathways, coordinating the expression of related enzymes and associated factors implicated in serine biosynthesis, one-carbon, and 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA) cycles.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study (Kosti et al., 2020).

claim: SERBP1 impacts methionine production and, consequently histone methylation and the expression of genes implicated in neuronal differentiation.
source: Ultimately, SERBP1 impacts methionine production and, consequently histone methylation and the expression of genes implicated in neuronal differentiation (Kosti et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Pull down experiments in 293T cells followed by proteomics analysis yielded a high-confidence list of 570 SERBP1-associated proteins.
source: Analysis by mass spectrometry yielded a high-confidence list of 570 SERBP1-associated proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from proteomics analysis described in the methods and results sections.

claim: 146 SERBP1 interactors identified in the study were also identified in other high-throughput studies.
source: 146 SERBP1 interactors identified in our analysis were also identified in other high-throughput studies – Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published datasets from Go et al., 2021; Youn et al., 2018 and BioGRID.

claim: SERBP1 participates in diverse regulatory complexes in the cytoplasm and nucleus.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analyses (Ge et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2019; Supek et al., 2011) of identified partners indicated that SERBP1 participates in diverse regulatory complexes in the cytoplasm and nucleus – Figure 1A and B and Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of proteomics data shown in Figure 1.

claim: SERBP1's partners indicate its participation in different stages of translation as well as in its regulation.
source: Although SERBP1's partners indicate its participation in different stages of translation as well as in its regulation, the many associations with translation initiation factors suggest that SERBP1's primary function is in initiation – Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomics data showing enrichment of translation initiation factors.

claim: SERBP1's primary function in translation is in initiation.
source: Although SERBP1's partners indicate its participation in different stages of translation as well as in its regulation, the many associations with translation initiation factors suggest that SERBP1's primary function is in initiation – Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomics data showing enrichment of translation initiation factors.

claim: Several ribosomal proteins are associated with SERBP1.
source: As expected, based on previous studies (Brown et al., 2018; Muto et al., 2018; Ahn et al., 2015; Martini et al., 2021), we identified several ribosomal proteins associated with SERBP1 – Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data and citations to previous studies.

claim: SERBP1 knockdown in U251 and U343 cells resulted in a decrease of overall translation as shown by puromycin incorporation assays.
source: SERBP1 knockdown in U251 and U343 cells resulted in a decrease of overall translation as shown by puromycin incorporation assays – Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from puromycin incorporation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: SERBP1 is mostly localized in the cytoplasm.
source: SERBP1 is mostly localized in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about SERBP1 localization.

claim: SERBP1 nuclear localization increases in response to stress and is regulated by arginine methyltransferases.
source: SERBP1 nuclear localization increases in response to stress and is regulated by arginine methyltransferases (Lee et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2012; Passos et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Out of 570 SERBP1-associated proteins, 344 display cytoplasmic/nuclear localization, while 100 are exclusively found in the nucleus.
source: SERBP1-associated proteins suggest it participates in nuclear functions; out of 570 associated proteins, 344 display cytoplasmic/nuclear localization, while 100 are exclusively found in the nucleus – Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the proteomics data.

claim: The functions of SERBP1-associated proteins suggest that SERBP1 is involved in different stages of ribosome biogenesis.
source: The functions of SERBP1-associated proteins suggest that SERBP1 is involved in different stages of ribosome biogenesis – Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This is inferred from GO analysis of SERBP1-associated proteins.

claim: SERBP1 participation in ribosome biogenesis is corroborated by its presence in nucleoli.
source: SERBP1 participation in ribosome biogenesis is corroborated by its presence in nucleoli – Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing SERBP1 localization in nucleoli.

claim: SERBP1 binds preferentially to multiple snoRNAs.
source: Results of our previous RIP-Seq analysis (Kosti et al., 2020) and a CLIP-seq study (Martini et al., 2021) showed that SERBP1 binds preferentially to multiple snoRNAs (Supplementary file 2) and at specific sites in 18 S and 28 S rRNA.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous RIP-Seq and CLIP-seq studies.

claim: SERBP1 binds at specific sites in 18 S and 28 S rRNA.
source: Results of our previous RIP-Seq analysis (Kosti et al., 2020) and a CLIP-seq study (Martini et al., 2021) showed that SERBP1 binds preferentially to multiple snoRNAs (Supplementary file 2) and at specific sites in 18 S and 28 S rRNA.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous RIP-Seq and CLIP-seq studies.

claim: SERBP1 associates with FBL and DKC1, two critical snoRNP components.
source: These results, aligned with the fact that SERBP1 associates with FBL and DKC1, two critical snoRNP components, strongly indicate SERBP1 involvement in rRNA modification.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data identifying FBL and DKC1 as SERBP1 interactors.

claim: SERBP1 is involved in rRNA modification.
source: These results, aligned with the fact that SERBP1 associates with FBL and DKC1, two critical snoRNP components, strongly indicate SERBP1 involvement in rRNA modification.
evidence: This is inferred from SERBP1's association with snoRNP components and binding to snoRNAs.

claim: SERBP1 is likely involved in different stages of RNA processing, in particular splicing, and telomere maintenance.
source: Besides ribosome biogenesis, SERBP1 is also likely involved in different stages of RNA processing, in particular splicing, and telomere maintenance – Figure 1A and B.
evidence: This is inferred from GO analysis of SERBP1-associated proteins shown in Figure 1.

claim: SERBP1 is a highly conserved protein.
source: SERBP1 is a highly conserved protein.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about SERBP1.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, SERBP1 homolog is STM1.
source: In S. cerevisiae, SERBP1 homolog is STM1 (Coppolecchia et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: 183 proteins were identified as STM1 interactors according to BioGRID.
source: According to BioGRID (Stark et al., 2006), 183 proteins were identified as STM1 interactors.
evidence: This is based on data from the BioGRID database.

claim: Of the 144 identified human homologs of STM1 interactors, 53 were SERBP1 interactors.
source: Of the 144 identified human homologs, we found that 53 were SERBP1 interactors – Supplementary file 3.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the SERBP1 interactome with STM1 interactors.

claim: Several regulatory functions assigned to SERBP1 based on its associated proteins are evolutionarily conserved, including translation, ribosome biogenesis, RNA processing and telomere maintenance.
source: Comparisons of enriched GO terms from the SERBP1 and STM1 analyses suggest that several regulatory functions assigned to SERBP1 based on its associated proteins are evolutionarily conserved, including translation, ribosome biogenesis, RNA processing and telomere maintenance – Supplementary file 3.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of GO analyses of SERBP1 and STM1 interactors.

claim: SERBP1 has homologs in plants.
source: SERBP1 also has homologs in plants.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about SERBP1 conservation.

claim: AtRGG proteins (SERBP1 homologs) in A. thaliana interact with ribosomal proteins and proteins involved in RNA processing and transport.
source: A recent study in A. thaliana established that AtRGG proteins (SERBP1 homologs) interact with ribosomal proteins and proteins involved in RNA processing and transport (Bleckmann et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: RNA binding and helicase are the two domain families that appeared most often among SERBP1-associated proteins.
source: In order to define the characteristics of SERBP1-associated proteins, we cataloged them according to their protein domains using the Pfam database (Sonnhammer et al., 1997) and performed an enrichment analysis. RNA binding and helicase are the two domain families that appeared most often – Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 4.
evidence: This is based on domain enrichment analysis of proteomics data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DDX21, DHX9, and DHX15 are SERBP1's top-associated helicases based on proteomics analyses and gene expression correlation studies.
source: Based on the results of the proteomics analyses and gene expression correlation studies, DDX21, DHX9, and DHX15 are SERBP1's top-associated helicases – Supplementary file 5.
evidence: This is based on proteomics data and expression correlation analysis.

claim: SERBP1 displays large intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs).
source: SERBP1 displays large intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs; Baudin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Roughly 80% of SERBP1-associated proteins contain IDRs.
source: Roughly 80% of SERBP1-associated proteins contain IDRs (Piovesan et al., 2023) and are present in different membraneless organelles, as discussed below – Figure 1D and Supplementary file 4.
evidence: This is based on analysis of SERBP1-associated proteins using the MobiDB database, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SERBP1 is a G-quadruplex (G4) binder.
source: SERBP1 is a G-quadruplex (G4) binder (Kosti et al., 2020; Su et al., 2021b), as are 38% of its associated proteins (Su et al., 2021b; Herviou et al., 2020) – Supplementary file 6.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 38% of SERBP1-associated proteins are G4 binders.
source: SERBP1 is a G-quadruplex (G4) binder (Kosti et al., 2020; Su et al., 2021b), as are 38% of its associated proteins (Su et al., 2021b; Herviou et al., 2020) – Supplementary file 6.
evidence: This is based on analysis of SERBP1-associated proteins against published G4 binder datasets.

claim: RBPs, including SERBP1, often use RGG boxes to bind G4 motifs.
source: RBPs, including SERBP1, often use RGG boxes to bind G4 motifs (Huang et al., 2018; Patra et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Among 93 SERBP1-associated proteins containing RGG boxes, 44 are G4 binders.
source: We found that among 93 SERBP1-associated proteins containing RGG boxes (Thandapani et al., 2013), 44 are G4 binders – Figure 1E and Supplementary file 6.
evidence: This is based on analysis of SERBP1-associated proteins shown in Figure 1E.

claim: G4 binders associated with SERBP1 are mostly proteins implicated in translation, mRNA stability, and splicing.
source: G4 binders associated with SERBP1 are mostly proteins implicated in translation, mRNA stability, and splicing, indicating that SERBP1 regulation via G4 binding takes place in different scenarios.
evidence: This is inferred from functional analysis of G4-binding SERBP1 interactors.

claim: Several RNA helicases (e.g. DDX5, DDX21, DDX3X, and DHX9) that are G4 binders enhance translation by unfolding G4s in 5' UTRs.
source: Among G4 binders, we identified several RNA helicases (e.g. DDX5, DDX21, DDX3X, and DHX9) that enhance translation by unfolding G4s in 5' UTRs (Herdy et al., 2018; McRae et al., 2020; Murat et al., 2018; Varshney et al., 2021) – Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1 and Supplementary file 6.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and proteomics data.

claim: Since SERBP1 lacks helicase domains, interaction with helicases could be critical for SERBP1 function in translation.
source: Since SERBP1 lacks helicase domains, interaction with these proteins could be critical for SERBP1 function in translation.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that SERBP1 lacks helicase domains but associates with helicases.

claim: G4s regulate different aspects of the life cycles of RNA viruses.
source: G4s regulate different aspects of the life cycles of RNA viruses (Ruggiero and Richter, 2018; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GO terms related to viral translation are among those with the highest fold enrichment in the SERBP1 interactome analyses.
source: GO terms related to viral translation are among those with the highest fold enrichment in our analyses – Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis of SERBP1-associated proteins.

claim: In a study to define the SARS-CoV-2 RNA interactome, 168 human proteins were identified (after exclusion of ribosomal proteins and EI3F factors), including SERBP1 and 92 of its associated proteins.
source: In a study to define the SARS-CoV-2 RNA interactome, 168 human proteins were identified (after exclusion of ribosomal proteins and EI3F factors; Lee et al., 2021), including SERBP1 and 92 of its associated proteins – Supplementary file 6.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published SARS-CoV-2 interactome data.

claim: Of the 92 SERBP1-associated proteins in the SARS-CoV-2 RNA interactome, 52 are G4 binders.
source: Of those 92 proteins, 52 are G4 binders – Supplementary file 6.
evidence: This is based on analysis of SERBP1-associated proteins.

claim: SERBP1 has been previously implicated in chromosome segregation and shown to localize in M bodies during mitosis.
source: SERBP1 has been previously implicated in chromosome segregation and shown to localize in M bodies during mitosis (Martini et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: GO analyses of SERBP1-associated proteins revealed chromosome segregation as well as several related functions as enriched terms.
source: In agreement, GO analyses of SERBP1-associated proteins revealed chromosome segregation as well as several related functions as enriched terms.
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis of proteomics data.

claim: SERBP1 interacts with proteins in chromosomes as well as centrosomes and mitotic spindles.
source: Examination of proteins linked to these terms indicated that SERBP1 interacts with proteins in chromosomes as well as centrosomes and mitotic spindles – Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This is based on analysis of SERBP1-associated proteins shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SERBP1 knockdown cells had markedly increased numbers of polynucleated cells after paclitaxel treatment, reflecting mitotic catastrophe.
source: In both cases, SERBP1 knockdown cells had markedly increased numbers of polynucleated cells, reflecting mitotic catastrophe – Figure 2B–D.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from paclitaxel treatment experiments shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: SERBP1 involvement in cell division appears to be conserved.
source: SERBP1 involvement in cell division appears to be conserved.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with yeast STM1 data.

claim: STM1, the SERBP1 yeast homolog, is a suppressor of mutations in genes regulating mitosis.
source: STM1, the SERBP1 yeast homolog, is a suppressor of mutations in genes regulating mitosis (Chung et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: GO analyses of STM1 genetic interactors showed enrichment for cell division.
source: Confirming that report, our GO analyses of STM1 genetic interactors showed enrichment for cell division – Supplementary file 3.
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of STM1 genetic interactors.

claim: SERBP1 overexpressing cells are less sensitive to drugs affecting cell division, cell cycle, and DNA replication.
source: Corroborating SERBP1 involvement in cell division, we determined that SERBP1 OE cells are less sensitive to drugs affecting cell division, cell cycle, and DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by drug screening data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Three drugs (Mitoxantrone, Flavopiridol, and Doxorubicin) that SERBP1 OE cells are less sensitive to are also known to affect rRNA transcription and processing.
source: Interestingly, three of these drugs (Mitoxantrone, Flavopiridol, and Doxorubicin) are also known to affect rRNA transcription and processing – Figure 2E and F and Supplementary file 7.
evidence: This is based on known properties of these drugs and drug screening data.

claim: Among identified SERBP1 partners, 134 proteins (23%) are implicated in mRNA processing, and from this group, 117 participate in mRNA splicing.
source: Among identified SERBP1 partners, 134 proteins (23%) are implicated in mRNA processing, and from this group, 117 participate in mRNA splicing.
evidence: This is based on functional analysis of SERBP1-associated proteins.

claim: SERBP1-associated proteins include many well-known alternative splicing regulators such as hnRNPU, KHDRBS1, PTBP1, SRSF6, TRA2B, SRSF2, and hnRNPA1.
source: They include many well-known alternative splicing regulators such as hnRNPU, KHDRBS1, PTBP1, SRSF6, TRA2B, SRSF2, and hnRNPA1 – Figure 3A.
evidence: This is based on proteomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: hnRNPU, TRA2B, and KHDRBS1 display high expression correlation with SERBP1 in multiple scenarios.
source: In particular, hnRNPU, TRA2B, and KHDRBS1 display high expression correlation with SERBP1 in multiple scenarios – Supplementary file 5.
evidence: This is based on expression correlation analysis.

claim: SERBP1 knockdown altered the splicing of 1,625 events (PSI >0.1, FRD <0.05) with 70% of them being exon skipping events.
source: SERBP1 knockdown altered the splicing of 1,625 events (PSI >0.1, FRD <0.05) with 70% of them being exon skipping events – Figure 3B and Supplementary file 8.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: From the 1625 splicing events altered in SERBP1 knockdown cells, CLIP sites were observed close to pertinent splice sites (<100 nucleotides) of 443 (27%) of them.
source: From the 1625 splicing events altered in SERBP1 knockdown cells, CLIP sites were observed close to pertinent splice sites (<100 nucleotides) of 443 (27%) of them – Figure 3C and Supplementary file 8.
evidence: This is based on analysis of CLIP-seq data in relation to splicing changes, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Circa 30% of the splicing events identified in SERBP1 knockdown cells were also observed upon hnRNPU knockdown, with changes in the same direction.
source: Circa 30% of the events identified in SERBP1 knockdown cells were also observed upon hnRNPU knockdown, with changes in the same direction – Figure 3E and F and Supplementary file 8.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data comparing SERBP1 and hnRNPU knockdowns shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: SERBP1 knockdown affects splicing events that include introns containing snoRNAs in 13 host genes.
source: Our analysis indicates that SERBP1 knockdown affects splicing events that include introns containing snoRNAs in 13 host genes – Supplementary file 8.
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: SERBP1 and PARP1 showed strong expression correlation in several scenarios and similar expression profiles during cortex development.
source: SERBP1 and PARP1 showed strong expression correlated in several scenarios and similar expression profiles during cortex development – Figure 4B and C, Supplementary file 5.
evidence: This is based on expression correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: PARP1 is implicated in DNA repair and regulates multiple stages of gene expression, including transcription, splicing, ribosome biogenesis, and translation.
source: PARP1 is implicated in DNA repair and regulates multiple stages of gene expression, including transcription, splicing, ribosome biogenesis, and translation (Kim et al., 2020; Gupte et al., 2017; Huang and Kraus, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SERBP1 gets PARylated and binds to PAR.
source: Results of high throughput studies established that SERBP1 gets PARylated and binds to PAR (Gibson et al., 2016; Martello et al., 2016; Dasovich et al., 2021) – Figure 4D, Supplementary file 6.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous high-throughput studies.

claim: SERBP1 PARylation by PARP1 was confirmed in an in vitro assay.
source: SERBP1 PARylation by PARP1 was confirmed in an in vitro assay – Figure 4E.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in vitro PARylation assay shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Circa 56% of all identified SERBP1 interactors get PARylated and/or bind PAR.
source: Moreover, we determined that circa 56% of all identified SERBP1 interactors get PARylated and/or bind PAR (Figure 4F, Supplementary file 6), suggesting that PARylation is an important component in the assembly of protein complexes in which SERBP1 participates.
evidence: This is based on analysis of SERBP1-associated proteins shown in Figure 4F.

claim: PARylation is an important component in the assembly of protein complexes in which SERBP1 participates.
source: Moreover, we determined that circa 56% of all identified SERBP1 interactors get PARylated and/or bind PAR (Figure 4F, Supplementary file 6), suggesting that PARylation is an important component in the assembly of protein complexes in which SERBP1 participates.
evidence: This is inferred from the high percentage of PARylated/PAR-binding proteins among SERBP1 interactors.

claim: Cell exposure to H2O2 enhances PARP1 activity and protein PARylation.
source: Cell exposure to H2O2 enhances PARP1 activity and protein PARylation as shown by Western blots probed with an anti-poly-ADP-ribose binding reagent – Figure 4G.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: In U251 cells, H2O2 treatment caused SERBP1 to shift to the nucleus, where it co-localized with PARP1.
source: In U251 cells, H2O2 treatment caused SERBP1 to shift to the nucleus, where it co-localized with PARP1 – Figure 4—figure supplement 1.
